strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: node classification with extremely imbalanced supervision. Retrieving existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing features and graph topology, and the framework accommodates multiple GNN architectures.

The experimental coverage is substantial: five datasets, three GNN architectures, imbalance ratios up to 100, and naturally imbalanced settings. Reported improvements are often meaningful; for example, Cora-GCN at ratio 20 improves F1 from the strongest listed baseline's 66.82 to 74.15.

The investigations of minority-class pseudo-label errors, clustering/classifier agreement, and geometric ranking provide useful empirical insights beyond aggregate benchmark performance. Component ablations and sensitivity analyses are also included.

The high-level pipeline is understandable, and the appendix documents architectures, optimization, hyperparameter ranges, dataset construction, and hardware. No material ethical concern is apparent from the benchmark study.
weaknesses: The closest prior method is missing from the evaluation. Section 6 acknowledges that M3S already filters pseudo-labels through agreement with embedding-space clustering, closely overlapping DPAM. Without a matched comparison against M3S, the incremental contribution of UNREAL is insufficiently established. Comparisons against ordinary self-training and graph oversampling methods do not resolve this central novelty and validation gap.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the supporting analyses. Table 9 reports 94.20 ± 8.04 as mean accuracy and standard error over five repetitions for Cora-GraphSAGE at ratio 50. Under that protocol, five accuracies bounded by 100 with mean 94.20 can have standard error at most 5.80. Table 7's GAT row at ratio 20 also reports aligned and discarded counts summing to 2613, despite listing 2625 unlabeled nodes. These may be reporting errors, but corrected tables and per-run results are needed.

The algorithm requires a more precise specification. Equation (5) measures distance to the assigned class center, whereas Section 4.3 treats that center as necessarily the nearest one. Assigning labels through cluster centers in Equation (4) does not guarantee this property for individual nodes. Algorithm 1 also does not explicitly enforce the per-class quota or update the unlabeled pool, and the minority-only selection schedule remains unclear. The manuscript provides search ranges but no implementation link or selected configurations to resolve these ambiguities.

The ablations do not fully establish the value of the proposed refinements. Table 11 retains DPAM throughout, and RBO-based fusion is not compared with simple fixed-weight rank fusion. DGIN sometimes reduces downstream performance, including CiteSeer-GraphSAGE F1 from 58.71 to 57.51. Claims of consistently superior performance also overlook losses on Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and Flickr balanced accuracy with GAT.

Computational advantages are insufficiently quantified. The search includes 40–100 training rounds, each allowing up to 2000 epochs, together with repeated clustering. End-to-end runtime, peak memory, and comparisons under matched computational budgets are absent. Flickr out-of-memory observations alone do not establish general efficiency, and attributing ReNode's memory failure to synthetic-node generation is incorrect.

The imbalance study confounds several factors. Table 13 increases majority-class labels from 20 to 50 to 100 while keeping minority classes at one label, and the citation-network training split changes for the larger ratios. Consequently, cross-ratio trends do not isolate imbalance from supervision budget and split effects. The naturally imbalanced experiments are useful, but provide less support for claims about extremely rare classes throughout the unlabeled population. Together with the missing closest baseline and unresolved reporting inconsistencies, these concerns outweigh the promising reported gains.
